Assume that either ZFC or NBG is inconsistent. Then the inconsistent theory implies the contradictory statements ∅&nbsp;=&nbsp;∅ and ∅&nbsp;≠&nbsp;∅, which are statements about sets. By the conservative extension property, the other theory also implies these statements. Therefore, it is also inconsistent. So although NBG is more expressive, it is equiconsistent with ZFC. This result together with von Neumann's 1929 relative consistency proof implies that his 1925 axiom system with the axiom of limitation of size is equiconsistent with ZFC. This completely resolves [[#von Neumann's concern|von Neumann's concern]] about the relative consistency of this powerful axiom since ZFC is within the Cantorian framework.

Even though NBG is a conservative extension of ZFC, a theorem may have a shorter and more elegant proof in NBG than in ZFC (or vice versa). For a survey of known results of this nature, see {{harvnb|Pudlák|1998}}.

[[Morse–Kelley set theory]] has an axiom schema of class comprehension that includes formulas whose quantifiers range over classes. MK is a stronger theory than NBG because MK proves the consistency of NBG,<ref>{{harvnb|Mostowski|1950|p=113}}, footnote 11. Footnote references [[Hao Wang (academic)|Wang]]'s NQ set theory, which later evolved into MK.</ref> while [[Gödel's second incompleteness theorem]] implies that NBG cannot prove the consistency of NBG.

For a discussion of some [[ontology|ontological]] and other philosophical issues posed by NBG, especially when contrasted with ZFC and MK, see Appendix C of {{harvnb|Potter|2004}}.

===Models===
ZFC, NBG, and MK have [[Model (mathematical logic)|model]]s describable in terms of the [[cumulative hierarchy]] ''V''<sub>''α''</sub>{{space|hair}} and the [[constructible hierarchy]] ''L''<sub>''α''</sub>{{space|hair}}. Let  ''V'' include an [[inaccessible cardinal]] κ, let ''X'' ⊆ ''V<sub>κ</sub>'', and let Def(''X'') denote the class of [[definable set|first-order definable subset]]s of ''X'' with parameters. In symbols where "<math>(X,\in)</math>" denotes the model with [[Model (mathematical logic)#domain|domain]] <math>X</math> and relation <math>\in</math>, and "<math>\models</math>" denotes the [[Model (mathematical logic)#Satisfaction relation|satisfaction relation]]:
<math display="block">\operatorname{Def}(X) := \Bigl\{ \{ x \mid x \in X \text{ and } (X,\in) \models \phi(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n) \}: \phi \text{ is a first-order formula and } y_{1},\ldots,y_{n} \in X \Bigr\}.</math>

Then:
* <math>(V_\kappa,\in)</math> and <math>(L_\kappa,\in)</math> are models of [[ZFC]].<ref>{{harvnb|Kanamori|2009b|pp=18, 29}}.</ref>
* (''V''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;''V''<sub>κ+1</sub>,&nbsp;∈) is a model of MK where ''V''<sub>κ</sub> consists of the sets of the model and ''V''<sub>κ+1</sub> consists of the classes of the model.<ref>{{harvnb|Chuaqui|1981|p=313}} proves that (''V''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;''V''<sub>κ+1</sub>,&nbsp;∈) is a model of MKTR + AxC. MKT is Tarski's axioms for MK without Choice or Replacement. MKTR + AxC is MKT with Replacement and Choice ({{harvnb|Chuaqui|1981|pp=4, 125}}), which is equivalent to MK.</ref> Since a model of MK is a model of NBG, this model is also a model of NBG. 
* (''V''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;Def(''V''<sub>κ</sub>),&nbsp;∈) is a model of Mendelson's version of NBG, which replaces NBG's axiom of global choice with ZFC's axiom of choice.<ref>{{harvnb|Mendelson|1997|p=275}}.</ref> The axioms of ZFC are true in this model because (''V''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;∈) is a model of ZFC. In particular, ZFC's axiom of choice holds, but NBG's global choice may fail.{{efn|Easton built a [[Axiom of limitation of size#Easton's choice model|model of Mendelson's version of NBG]] in which ZFC's axiom of choice holds but global choice fails.}} NBG's class existence axioms are true in this model because the classes whose existence they assert can be defined by first-order definitions. For example, the membership axiom holds since the class <math>E</math> is defined by: <math display="block">E = \{x \in V_\kappa: (V_\kappa,\in) \models \exists u  \ \exists v [x = (u, v) \land u \in v]\}.</math>
* (''L''<sub>κ</sub>, ''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>, ∈), where κ<sup>+</sup> is the [[successor cardinal]] of κ, is a model of NBG.{{efn|In the cumulative hierarchy V<sub>κ</sub>, the subsets of V<sub>κ</sub> are in V<sub>κ+1</sub>. The constructible hierarchy ''L''<sub>κ</sub> produces subsets more slowly, which is why the subsets of ''L''<sub>κ</sub> are in ''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub> rather than ''L''<sub>κ+1</sub>.<ref>{{harvnb|Gödel|1940|p=54}}; {{harvnb|Solovay|1990|pp=9&ndash;11}}.</ref>}} NBG's class existence axioms are true in (''L''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>,&nbsp;∈). For example, the membership axiom holds since the class <math>E</math> is defined by: <math display="block">E = \{x \in L_\kappa: (L_\kappa,\in) \models \exists u  \ \exists v [x = (u, v) \land u \in v]\}.</math> So ''E''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;𝒫(''L''<sub>κ</sub>). In his proof that [[generalized continuum hypothesis|GCH]] is true in ''L'', Gödel proved that 𝒫(''L''<sub>κ</sub>)&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>.<ref>{{harvnb|Gödel|1940|p=54}}.</ref> Therefore, ''E''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>, so the membership axiom is true in (''L''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>,&nbsp;∈). Likewise, the other class existence axioms are true. The axiom of global choice is true because ''L''<sub>κ</sub> is well-ordered by the [[Restriction (mathematics)|restriction]] of [[#Gödel's function|Gödel's function]] (which maps the class of ordinals to the constructible sets) to the ordinals less than κ. Therefore, (''L''<sub>κ</sub>,&nbsp;''L''<sub>κ<sup>+</sup></sub>,&nbsp;∈) is a model of NBG.
* If <math>M</math> is a [[Standard model (set theory)|nonstandard model]] of <math>\mathrm{ZFC}</math>, then <math>(M,\mathrm{Def}(M))\vDash \mathrm{NBG}+\Delta^1_1\text{-CA}</math> is equivalent to "there exists an <math>X</math> such that <math>(M,X)\vDash\mathrm{NBG}+\Delta^1_1\text{-CA}</math>", where <math>\mathrm{Def}(M)</math> is the set of subsets of <math>M</math> that are definable over <math>M</math>.<ref>A. Enayat, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168007222000732 Set theoretical analogues of the Barwise-Schlipf theorem]". Annals of Pure and Applied Logic vol. 173 (2022).</ref> This provides a second-order part for extending a given first-order nonstandard model of <math>\mathrm{ZFC}</math> to a nonstandard model of <math>\mathrm{NBG}</math>, if there is such an extension at all.

==Category theory==
The ontology of NBG provides scaffolding for speaking about "large objects" without risking paradox. For instance, in some developments of [[category theory]], a "[[large category]]" is defined as one whose [[object (category theory)|object]]s and [[morphism]]s make up a proper class. On the other hand, a "small category" is one whose objects and morphisms are members of a set. Thus, we can speak of the "[[category of all sets]]" or "[[category of all small categories]]" without risking paradox since NBG supports large categories.

However, NBG does not support a "category of all categories" since large categories would be members of it and NBG does not allow proper classes to be members of anything. An ontological extension that enables us to talk formally about such a "category" is the [[Conglomerate (mathematics)|conglomerate]], which is a collection of classes. Then the "category of all categories" is defined by its objects: the conglomerate of all (large) categories; and its morphisms: the conglomerate of all morphisms from ''A'' to ''B'' where ''A'' and ''B'' are objects.<ref>{{harvnb|Adámek|Herrlich|Strecker|2004|pp=15&ndash;16, 40}}.</ref> On whether an ontology including classes as well as sets is adequate for category theory, see {{harvnb|Muller|2001}}.
